OK Boomer is a cooperative survival horror game developed by Pugsy Studios and published by GameDev.ist that takes an imaginative approach to multiplayer horror by transporting players into a warped version of the internet where corrupted code, digital anomalies, and terrifying entities lurk around every corner. Instead of relying on traditional zombie outbreaks or haunted locations, the game embraces a cyber-themed nightmare filled with unstable environments and bizarre supernatural threats. Its unusual premise immediately gives it a unique identity, especially for players looking for a horror experience that blends retro technology with modern internet-inspired concepts. Designed primarily for online cooperative play, the game encourages up to four players to work together while investigating dangerous virtual landscapes. Success depends less on individual skill and more on effective communication, careful exploration, and coordinated teamwork. Every expedition demands that players search for objectives, manage limited resources, and react quickly to unpredictable dangers. The cooperative structure ensures that every participant has an important role, making victories feel rewarding while mistakes can quickly spiral into tense and chaotic situations. One of the game's most creative mechanics is its use of outdated analog equipment as the primary means of combating digital horrors. Rather than equipping players with powerful futuristic weapons, OK Boomer challenges them to rely on vintage devices to identify, weaken, and eliminate corrupted entities. This gameplay choice reinforces the game's central theme while creating memorable encounters that feel different from the combat systems commonly found in other cooperative horror titles. The contrast between obsolete technology and advanced digital nightmares is both humorous and unsettling, helping the game establish a memorable personality. The environments also contribute significantly to the overall atmosphere. Players venture through distorted digital spaces filled with visual glitches, corrupted architecture, and eerie audiovisual effects that constantly reinforce the feeling of exploring a broken network. The monsters are inspired by corrupted data and internet folklore instead of conventional horror creatures, giving each encounter a strange and unpredictable quality. Combined with limited resources and the constant threat of losing control of the situation, the game maintains an effective sense of suspense throughout each mission. Replay value appears to be another strength thanks to the cooperative design and dynamic gameplay. Every session encourages players to refine their strategies, improve communication, and experiment with different ways of overcoming increasingly dangerous scenarios. Since much of the experience depends on player interaction and teamwork rather than scripted sequences, repeated playthroughs remain engaging as different groups develop their own tactics and approaches. This emphasis on cooperation makes the game particularly appealing for friends who enjoy solving problems together while facing mounting pressure. As an Early Access title, OK Boomer already presents a promising foundation while leaving room for future improvements and additional content. The developers have established a distinctive concept that stands apart from many multiplayer horror games by combining retro technology, internet mythology, survival mechanics, and cooperative gameplay into a cohesive experience. Although players should expect continued refinement as development progresses, the core gameplay loop already demonstrates considerable creativity and potential for long-term growth. Overall, OK Boomer delivers an inventive take on cooperative survival horror by combining atmospheric exploration, teamwork, resource management, and an unconventional digital setting. Its creative mechanics and distinctive visual theme help it avoid feeling like a generic multiplayer horror game, while its emphasis on collaboration provides satisfying moments of tension and accomplishment. Players who appreciate cooperative horror experiences with fresh ideas and a strong thematic identity will likely find plenty to enjoy, especially as the game continues to evolve through future updates. Rating: 7/10

Boring gameplay loop, very few enemies to encounter, and too easy to make quota. Bad sound balancing, going from not that loud to way too loud. I also had performance issues, generally low fps (60fps at best? I know I'm on 1440p but I get higher fps in cyberpunk) with constant framedrops. Are there good things here? Eh unsure, there are some fun references of course, the idea behind the enemies that do exist aren't bad, just not too original. There is a selection of weapons and items, but nothing out of the ordinary. There is an upgrade system and multiple maps available, but nothing that truly affects the core gameplay loop in a meaningful way. You go in, encounter the same 7 enemies in rooms that are either too cramped or too open, get completely body blocked by your friends in every door, suck some glitches, and repeat. There is no scare factor because the enemies are around every corner. If you really want to try this game, get it on sale, try it out, and like me, probably refund it within 2 hours.

I don't get jump scared, even though I'm a scaredy cat, the monsters are dull, and honestly I don't think it's very fun. I really hope to see that this game thrives in the future, and there are plenty of people who I'm sure love it. This game just wasn't my cup of tea and i'm sad. Maybe it's because I've gotten used to repo and lethal company after they already grew and thrived, and I'm just not ready to start over with another game from the very beginning. I'd say wait to purchase, but also support your developers. Developers you have a lot of your work cut out for you, and I really hope this game makes it to the top some day and you can all make fun of my comment.
